headline: Forecasters traded a stormy, wet week for a cool, dry stretch ahead.
summary:
The week began with forecasters expecting a conveyor belt of Pacific storms, all fed by a deep low-pressure area far out over the northeast Pacific. They called for a wet, windy week, with the strongest storms Friday through Sunday. Wind advisories went up for the coast and northern lowlands early in the week, and the Skokomish River on the Olympic Peninsula, already running high, stayed a flood worry throughout. Midweek brought a brief mild, mostly dry break, possibly record-warm in Seattle on Thursday. The weekend storms stayed the main concern, though forecasters admitted the timing and strength of the second one were less certain. By Friday, the worst-case coastal winds were scaled back to advisory-level gusts.

The bigger shift was the pattern for the following week. From Thursday, forecasters said the storm track would move south and a "block" would set in, meaning a stubborn area of high pressure that parks over the West and steers storms away. Saturday brought some doubt, with a deep low possibly approaching the coast Wednesday. By Sunday they expected it to pass to the south, leaving western Washington cool and mostly dry from Wednesday night through Friday, with highs near 50 and some chilly nights. Rain could return next Saturday, but forecasters are unsure how much.

turning_points.what: The Skokomish River flood watch became a flood warning as the river rose, and storm timing was nudged to Thursday night and around Sunday.
Forecasters added a drier stretch later in the week from a stalled high-pressure block, and called the weekend storm less certain.
Possible storm-force coastal winds were scaled back to wind advisories, and the midweek dry-out was described more firmly.
After Saturday's doubt about a midweek low near the coast, forecasters settled on it passing south, leaving a cool, dry week.
